To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

families whose mothers were underemployed and unemployed/had involuntary gaps had heightened risks of material hardships, especially those that involved paying bills and having adequate health and housing.
families whose mothers are underemployed or have involuntary job gaps are more likely to have a bill-paying, health or housing hardship.

families headed by single mothers who are unemployed and underemployed are more likely than adequately employed single mothers to experience bill-paying, health care, housing, and food hardships, and these employment problems also were related to other family characteristics that increase the risk of experiencing material hardships.

understanding the relationship between employment problems (unemployment, underemployment) and material hardship in single-parent families.

the impact of employment problems on single-mother families, and we find that unemployment and underemployment are associated with heightened risks of experiencing a number of different types of material hardship.

unemployment and underemployment are associated with increased risk of experiencing material hardship among single mothers.
unemployment is a major cause of hardship for single mothers, and that underemployment is a major contributor to hardship for single mothers.
unemployment is the most significant factor in material hardship.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the more employment problems a family has, the more material hardship they will experience, but that the relationship between the two is not linear and that the type of hardship experienced may be differentially affected by the type of employment problem.
the more employment instability, the greater the material hardship.
employment problems, especially unemployment and involuntary job gaps, are associated with heightened risks of experiencing material hardships among single-mother family members.
The main takeaway from our work is that

social service and social policy professionals should be concerned about how unemployment, involuntary job gaps, and underemployment are related to hardship for single-mother families, and they should be concerned about the effects of hardship on the well-being of single mothers and their children.
social work practitioners and policymakers need to consider the material hardships experienced by single-mother families when designing and implementing interventions and programs.
social workers should be aware that employment problems, such as unemployment and underemployment, may be related to material hardship among single mothers.
